quote: Now, then, let us also inquire into this: what is the cause that a woman, who furnishes a ministry to those being born into this world, is said to be made "unclean" not only when "she has received seed," but also when "she has borne"? Whence also for her purification she is commanded to offer "young pigeons or turtledoves for sin at the door of the tabernacle of testimony," that "the priest may make propitiation for her," as one who owes a propitiation and a purification of sin for the fact that she furnished a ministry to a man being born into this world. For thus it is written: "And the priest shall make propitiation for her, and she shall be cleansed." That our Lord Jesus Christ is called a physician in the divine Scriptures we are fully taught by the sentence of the Lord himself, as he says in the Gospels: "They that are whole need not a physician, but they that are sick. For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." Now every physician compounds medicines beneficial to bodies from the juices of herbs or of trees, or even from the veins of metals or the natures of living creatures. But if someone should chance to look upon these herbs before they are compounded according to the reasoning of the art, then indeed, if they are in the fields or on the mountains, he tramples them underfoot and passes them by as worthless grass. "And the Lord spoke," it says, "unto Moses, saying: Speak unto the children of Israel, and thou shalt say unto them: Whatsoever woman shall have conceived seed and borne a male, she shall be unclean seven days." First let us consider according to the history, whether it does not seem to be added as though superfluously: "the woman who shall have conceived seed and borne a male," as if she could bear a male otherwise than by seed conceived. But it is not added superfluously. For to distinguish her who "conceived and bore" without seed, the lawgiver added this word for the sake of the other women, so that he might designate as "unclean" not every woman who had borne, but her who "had borne with seed conceived." It was certainly not for nothing that the commandment was given for the child "to be circumcised on the eighth day"; it can only have been because the rock, the stone with which we are circumcised, was Christ. It was "with knives of rock" or stone that the people were circumcised;"now the rock was Christ." So why on the eighth day? Because in seven-day weeks the first is the same as the eighth; once you've completed the seven days, you are back at the first. The seventh is finished, the Lord is buried; we are back at the first, the Lord is raised up. The Lord's resurrection, you see, promised us an eternal day and consecrated for us the Lord's day. It's called the Lord's because it properly belongs to the Lord, because on it the Lord rose again. The rock has been restored to us; let those be circumcised who wish to say, "For we are the circumcision."

Which Sabbath He in His body abolished, although, nevertheless, He had formerly Himself commanded Moses that circumcision should not pass over the eighth day, which day very frequently happens on the Sabbath, as we read written in the Gospel.

quote: But meanwhile she "who has borne a male," "on the eighth day" both the one who is born is circumcised and she is made clean. It is a matter of great labor for these things to happen in this brevity of time, yet, that we may say something in passing, this week may be seen as the time of the present life; for in a week of days the world was completed. In which, so long as we are set in the flesh, we cannot be pure to the point of clarity, unless the eighth day come, that is, unless the time of the age to come be present. On which day, however, he who is a male and has acted manfully is at once purified in the very coming of the age to come, and at once the mother who bore him is made clean; for she will receive the flesh purged of vices out of the resurrection. The Lord commanded in the law that those who could were to offer a lamb for a son or a daughter, along with a turtledove or a pigeon. But one who did not have sufficient wealth to offer a lamb should offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons. Therefore the Lord, mindful in everything of our salvation, not only deigned for our sake to become a human being, though he was God, but also he deigned to become poor for us, though he was rich, so that by his poverty along with his humanity he might grant us to become sharers in his riches and his divinity.
source_title: HOMILY XV. ON THE PURIFICATION OF BLESSED MARY
